summary: Contains definitions of managed objects used as experimental extensions to the generic interfaces structure of MIB-II. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1573.

eli5.summary: It adds more items to the list of things you can ask a network port about.

questions: what extensions were added to the generic interface mib
what is the generic interface mib extension
how do snmp interface tests work
subtitle: Experimental SNMP objects that add counters, self-tests and receive addresses to every network interface.

tldr.problem: Work on media-specific MIBs kept finding objects that every interface needs, and defining them in each media MIB would have repeated them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1229 defines three tables as experimental extensions to the generic interfaces group of MIB-II: an extension table, a test table and a receive address table.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1229 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 1239 and obsoleted by RFC 1573.

today: RFC 1229 was obsoleted by RFC 1573 and had been updated by RFC 1239. Its status was Proposed Standard, and the text describes its objects as experimental.

sections.title: Why Extend the Generic Interface Group
sections.content:
The Internet Standard MIB already has a group of objects for a device's network interfaces. These objects are generic: they apply to all interfaces regardless of media and protocol. Efforts to define MIBs for particular media found objects that are needed or useful but are not tied to one interface type.

To avoid repeating them in many media-specific MIBs, this memo defines them once, as extensions to the generic interface group. The memo is explicitly experimental. Its objects sit under ifExtensions, which is { experimental 6 }, and are written in the format of the SMI as amended by RFC 1212. It builds on the Network Management Framework of RFC 1155, RFC 1156, RFC 1213 and RFC 1157.
sections.eli5: Every network port has a basic information card. Some extra questions applied to every kind of port, so they were written once on a shared extra card.

sections.title: The Interface Extension Table
sections.content:
This table holds new objects that apply to all types of subnetwork interface, and the group is mandatory for all of them. It has one entry per interface, indexed by ifExtnsIfIndex, which has the same value as ifIndex for that interface.

The entries include ifExtnsChipSet, an object identifier naming the hardware chip set (the value { 0 0 } means unknown), and ifExtnsRevWare, a printable ASCII string of 0 to 255 characters for the firmware version. There are four counters of frames successfully transmitted or received to multicast or broadcast addresses. Finally, ifExtnsPromiscuous is true(1) when the interface accepts all frames on the media and false(2) when it accepts only frames addressed to the station. It is read-only, though implementors are encouraged to make it read-write where that makes sense.
sections.eli5: This card lists the port's chip, its software version, how many group messages and shout-to-everyone messages it sent and heard, and whether it listens to everything or only mail addressed to it.

sections.title: The Interface Test Table
sections.content:
This table lets a network manager tell an agent to test an interface. It is optional, but if it is implemented, all its objects must be. A manager writes a test identifier to ifExtnsTestType to start a test and writes noTest to abort one. The RFC itself assigns one test, a full-duplex loopback test, and leaves others to media-specific documents. Only one test can run on an interface at a time, and a second invoked test is rejected.

The outcome is read from ifExtnsTestResult, with more detail in ifExtnsTestCode. The agent also records who started the test in ifExtnsTestCommunity and ifExtnsTestRequestId, so a manager can notice if two managers' tests overlapped.

A management station must not retransmit a test request that gets no response. It should inspect the agent's MIB to see whether the test started. Some tests take the interface off-line or even reboot the agent, so the agent should try to answer before it loses contact, and the ifIndex value must not change across such a reboot.
sections.eli5: A manager can press a test button on a port and later read the result. Only one test can run on a port at a time, and if you do not hear back you should check whether it started instead of pressing again.

sections.title: The Receive Address Table
sections.content:
This table is mandatory for interfaces that can receive frames addressed to more than one address. It lists each broadcast, multicast or unicast address for which the system will accept frames on an interface. It is indexed by the interface and the address (ifExtnsRcvAddrIfIndex and ifExtnsRcvAddress). In promiscuous mode, entries are only required for addresses the system would receive for if it were not promiscuous.

Each entry's ifExtnsRcvAddrStatus can be read-write. The value nonVolatile(4) survives a restart, volatile(3) does not and is the default, other(1) is valid but unclassified, and setting invalid(2) removes the entry. Whether an invalidated entry is removed from the table is up to the agent, so managers must be prepared to see entries that are no longer in use.
sections.eli5: This is the guest list of addresses a port will accept mail for. Some names stay on the list after a restart, and others are crossed off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 1229 states that security issues are not discussed in the memo. The test table does record the SNMP community and request-id of whoever last started a test, but the memo does not present this as a security feature.
sections.eli5: The authors did not write anything about keeping this safe from bad guys.

items.label: notSupported
items.desc: The agent cannot perform the test.

items.label: unAbleToRun
items.desc: Not run because of the state of the system.
